LESSON: POPULATION STRUCTURE

Grade: Grade 9
Subject: SOCIAL STUDIES
Strand: People and Relationships
Topic 3.4: Population Structure

SECTION 1: WELCOME

Hello! This is a study lesson on Population Structure. Read the explanation, follow every worked example, then do the practice. This is original CBC Learn content written from KICD outcomes — not a copy of a commercial textbook.

Big question: Why is the population structure of a country important?

SECTION 2: WHAT YOU WILL LEARN

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

1. identify sources of population data in a country
2. explain factors determining population structure in Kenya and Germany
3. construct age-sex population pyramids of developed and developing countries

SECTION 3: STUDY NOTES (READ AND LEARN)

WHAT YOU ARE STUDYING: POPULATION STRUCTURE
Subject: SOCIAL STUDIES · Grade: Grade 9
This is a learner study lesson (not a teacher guide). Read every part, follow the models, then practise.

BIG PICTURE
Population Structure helps you succeed in SOCIAL STUDIES. You will understand it, practise it, and use it in your county, school, and Kenyan community.

KEY FACTS: POPULATION STRUCTURE
Good citizens follow rules, respect others, and care for shared places.
Kenyan examples: lining up, keeping the compound clean, telling the truth, helping a classmate.
Rights come with responsibilities.

PART 1: Identify sources of population data in a country

What this means
In this part you learn to identify sources of population data in a country. You will use ideas from in your county, school, and Kenyan community.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: identify sources of population data in a country.
2. Locate, explain, then act responsibly using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Locate: Connect “Population Structure” to a real place or group in Kenya (school, market, county office, home).

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can identify sources of population data in a country. Write or say your answer clearly.

PART 2: Explain factors determining population structure in Kenya and Germany

What this means
In this part you learn to explain factors determining population structure in Kenya and Germany. You will use ideas from in your county, school, and Kenyan community.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: explain factors determining population structure in Kenya and Germany.
2. Locate, explain, then act responsibly using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Explain: Give one cause and one effect linked to Population Structure.

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can explain factors determining population structure in Kenya and Germany. Write or say your answer clearly.

PART 3: Construct age-sex population pyramids of developed and developing countries

What this means
In this part you learn to construct age-sex population pyramids of developed and developing countries. You will use ideas from in your county, school, and Kenyan community.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: construct age-sex population pyramids of developed and developing countries.
2. Locate, explain, then act responsibly using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Participate: Describe one responsible action a Grade learner can take.

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can construct age-sex population pyramids of developed and developing countries. Write or say your answer clearly.

PUT IT TOGETHER
Close your notes and say aloud: what Population Structure is, one example, and one way you will practise this week.

SECTION 4: QUICK EXAMPLES

Good citizens follow rules, respect others, and care for shared places.

Kenyan examples: lining up, keeping the compound clean, telling the truth, helping a classmate.

Example 1: Connect “Population Structure” to a real place or group in Kenya (school, market, county office, home). (skill: identify sources of population data in a country)

Example 2: Give one cause and one effect linked to Population Structure. (skill: explain factors determining population structure in Kenya and Germany)

Example 3: Describe one responsible action a Grade learner can take. (skill: construct age-sex population pyramids of developed and developing countries)

SECTION 5: PRACTICE NOW

1. Write 5 sentences (or show 5 clear steps) that teach Population Structure to a classmate.
2. Practise this skill: identify sources of population data in a country.
3. Practise this skill: explain factors determining population structure in Kenya and Germany.
4. Practise this skill: construct age-sex population pyramids of developed and developing countries.
5. Make one local Kenya example of Population Structure from your county, market, farm, or school.
6. Mark your own work: What did you get right? What will you redo?

SECTION 6: WORK TO DO (HOME / REVISION)

1. In your exercise book, make a one-page revision sheet for Population Structure: meaning, 3 examples, 5 practice items.
2. Teach a parent/guardian or younger sibling one part of this lesson (2 minutes).
3. Answer in writing: Why should a Grade 9 learner study Population Structure?
4. Prepare for the quiz: cover the Remember box and recite it.

SECTION: THINK ABOUT IT

1. Why is the population structure of a country important?

SECTION: REMEMBER

1. Know what Population Structure means in your own words.
2. Use local Kenyan examples, not only definitions.
3. Practise in small steps, then check your work.
4. Be able to: identify sources of population data in a country.
5. Be able to: explain factors determining population structure in Kenya and Germany.

Now complete the Revision Quiz. Open Answers only after you finish.

— CBC Learn · Original study notes from KICD outcomes (Strategy 2)
